What the water carries, what the boat makes, and how to tell them apart.
Where the boat is, how old that answer is, and how wrong it is allowed to be.
Water in the boat — finding it, stopping it, and knowing whether you are winning.
Fire aboard is an electrical problem until the power is proved gone.
The air is a system with sources, sinks and a flow path, and people are in it.
What turns the shaft, what cools it, and what the boat gives away by running it.
Sonar Supervisor

Runs the sonar room, which is a dark space with three displays and one
rule: the loudest thing on the screen is almost never the thing that
matters. He has eleven years of watches and can tell you what a fishing
fleet sounds like at four thousand yards.

Sound in water is not like light in air. It bends toward the colder,
slower water, so a layer of warm surface water above a cold one makes a
shadow zone the boat can hide in — and so can everybody else. A contact
that vanishes has not necessarily left; it may have crossed the layer.

His limit is that passive sonar gives him bearing and almost nothing
else. Range and course have to be built up by watching how the bearing
changes over time, which is why he will not give a track from one look and
gets short with anybody who asks for one.
Why can a contact disappear from Rask's display without going anywhere?
Sound bends toward colder water, into a shadow zone
Passive sonar stops working when a contact slows down
The array can only hold four contacts at a time
A contact that stops making noise ceases to reflect sound
What does passive sonar give Rask directly?
A bearing, and almost nothing else until he watches it change
A range, from the strength of the sound
A course and speed, from the frequency alone
A depth, from the angle the sound arrives at
Broadband Operator

Sits the broadband stack for six hours at a stretch, which is a job of
listening to noise and noticing when a shape appears in it. Two years
aboard, and better at it than people twice her time.

The display she watches is bearing against time, and the thing she is
looking for is a line that persists. A single bright mark is nothing —
the sea is full of them. A faint mark in the same place minute after
minute is a contact, because the sea has no reason to be consistent.

She keeps a paper log of what the boat itself was doing when a trace
appeared, because half the traces that frighten a new operator are the
boat's own: a pump that started, a shaft that came up in turns, a hull
popping as the depth changed.
What makes Dunne treat a faint mark as a real contact?
It stays on the same bearing while random marks do not
It is brighter than the marks around it
It appears at the same time as a hull pop
It shows on two displays fed by the same array
Navigator

Keeps the plot, and holds the only opinion on this boat that the captain
cannot overrule with an order: how well the plot is known. Her working
rule is that a position is a claim with an age on it, and the age is the
part everybody forgets to ask about.

Submerged, the boat navigates by dead reckoning — a course, a speed, and a
clock, drawn forward from the last position that came from a measurement.
That line is exactly as good as its assumptions, and it knows nothing
about the water it is drawn on. A half-knot current running for four hours
is two miles the plot will never mention.

So she draws the uncertainty as a circle and grows it with time, and picks
routes that survive being wrong rather than routes that are safe if she is
right. The bottom is her favourite instrument, because a depth sounding is
the one thing aboard that cannot be wrong for the same reason the plot is.
What does Sowande mean by the age of a position?
How long since the position came from a measurement
How long the chart itself has been aboard
How long the boat has been submerged on this patrol
How long the plot takes to redraw at a new speed
Why does she treat a depth sounding as her best instrument?
Nothing it depends on is also feeding the plot
It is more precise than any other instrument aboard
It gives a position directly, without a chart
It works at any speed, where other instruments do not
Assistant Navigator

Runs the chart table and the depth sounder, and is the person who actually
writes the time beside a fix. Nine years, four boats, and a handwriting
that anybody can read at two in the morning, which is not a small thing.

Her job is the arithmetic the plot depends on: set and drift, course made
good, speed of advance. She is the one who notices that a course steered
and a course made good have quietly diverged, because she is the one
comparing them.

What she guards against is the display that looks like a measurement and
is not. The chart overlay and the electronic repeat both draw from the
inertial navigator, so they agree perfectly and always will. Two displays
showing one source is not confirmation, and she will say so out loud.
Why is Petrov unimpressed when the chart overlay and the plot repeat agree?
Both come from the same inertial navigator
The overlay updates more slowly than the repeat does
They use different chart datums and should not be compared
Agreement between displays is only meaningful at periscope depth
Chief of the Boat, Damage Control

Runs damage control, which means he runs the drills nobody enjoys and owns
the compartments when something goes wrong in one. Twenty-two years. He
has been in a flooded space twice and does not tell either story.

The thing he teaches first is that water coming in through a hole under
pressure does not care how hard you pump. Flow through a hole goes up with
the square root of the pressure difference, and pressure goes up with
depth, so the same hole floods faster the deeper you are. Pumping buys
minutes; the hull fitting is what ends it.

His second rule is that a bilge level is not a number, it is a trend. One
reading tells you nothing. Two readings a minute apart tell you whether
you are winning, and that is the only question a flooding casualty is
actually asking.
Why does the same hole flood faster deeper?
Flow rises with pressure, and pressure rises with depth
Water is denser deeper, so more of it fits through
The hull flexes at depth and enlarges the hole
Pumps lose suction at depth, which only seems like faster flooding
What is Ferro's rule about a bilge level?
One reading is nothing; two a minute apart tell you
Any reading above the deck plate means abandon the compartment
The level matters less than the temperature of the water
A level that is not rising means the leak has stopped
Auxiliary Division, Pumps & Patches

Owns the drain pump, the portable pumps and the shoring locker, and can
put a patch on a split pipe in the dark, which she has had to prove more
than once during drills.

She thinks in rates rather than amounts. A pump is a number of gallons a
minute at a stated head, and that number falls as it has to lift water
further — so the same pump that empties a bilge on the surface struggles
at depth against a rising level. Knowing the two rates is knowing whether
to fight or to isolate.

Her standing complaint is that people start pumps before they find the
source, because starting a pump feels like doing something. It also
empties the compartment of the evidence that would have shown where the
water was coming in.
Why does Hallam object to starting a pump before finding the source?
It washes away the evidence of where the water enters
Pumps cannot run while a compartment is still flooding
Starting a pump early floods the bilge main
A pump run dry will not restart later
Electrical Division

Owns the switchboard, the breakers and every cable run on the boat, and
has the calmest voice in an emergency of anybody aboard, which is not an
accident — he practises it.

His subject is that an electrical fire is not a fire problem. It has three
legs: the fuel, which is cable insulation; the oxygen, which is the air in
the compartment; and the ignition source, which is an energized fault that
will keep re-lighting the fuel no matter what you spray on it. Take the
power away and it becomes an ordinary fire. Leave it on and it is a fire
that reflashes.

What he refuses to accept is a lamp as proof. A switchboard indicator says
what the switchboard believes, and a meter says what the cable is doing.
Between those two is where people get hurt, so isolation is not isolation
until it has been measured.
Why is spraying an energized electrical fire not enough?
The fault keeps re-lighting the insulation
The agent cannot reach a fire behind a panel
Electrical fires burn hotter than the agent can absorb
The smoke displaces the agent before it works
What does Okonkwo mean by "isolation is not isolation until it is measured"?
A lamp reports a belief, a meter reports the cable
Isolation has to be logged before it counts
Two people must witness a breaker being opened
A breaker is only isolated once the load has cooled
Power Distribution

Traces circuits, which sounds dull until the day it is the only thing that
matters. He keeps the dependency diagrams that say what each breaker feeds
and, more importantly, what stops when it opens.

Every isolation costs something downstream. Killing a bus to make a fire
safe also kills whatever that bus was feeding — a cooling pump, a scrubber
fan, a gyro. The decision is never whether to isolate; it is knowing what
you are turning off at the same time and in what order to bring it back.

Restoring is the part people rush. Loads come back in dependency order —
cooling before the thing that needs cooling, ventilation before the space
that needs it — and never onto a fault that has not been proved gone.
What does Mbeki's dependency diagram tell you that a breaker label does not?
What stops working elsewhere when that breaker opens
How much current the breaker will carry before tripping
Which compartment the cable physically runs through
How long the breaker takes to reset after a trip
Atmosphere Control Officer

Owns the air. On a submerged boat that means the scrubbers that take
carbon dioxide out, the generators that put oxygen in, the monitors that
say how it is going, and the ventilation that decides which compartments
any of it reaches.

Her subject is a balance. People produce carbon dioxide steadily, at a
rate that depends on how many of them are in the space and how hard they
are working. The scrubber removes it at a rate that depends on being able
to reach the air — which means the dampers. A compartment isolated from
the ventilation system has no scrubber, however healthy the plant looks.

What she insists on is the difference between a report and a measurement.
An installed sensor is a report from a device that may itself have failed;
a handheld reading taken in the space is a measurement. When the two
disagree the answer is not to average them.
Why can a compartment's air go bad while the scrubber plant reads healthy?
The scrubber only reaches compartments whose dampers are open
Scrubbers work more slowly at depth
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and sinks below the sensors
The plant reads its own outlet, which is always the cleanest air
An installed sensor and a handheld reading disagree. What does Lindqvist do?
Treats the handheld as the measurement and the sensor as a report that may have failed
Averages the two, since both are instruments
Believes the installed sensor, because it is calibrated more often
Waits for a third reading before doing anything
Corpsman

The only medical person aboard, which makes her the first instrument the
atmosphere has: people show symptoms before a monitor alarms, and she is
the one who hears about a headache in berthing.

She is careful about what a symptom proves. A headache and heavy breathing
in one compartment and not another is evidence about that compartment. The
same symptoms everywhere are evidence about the whole boat. Symptoms in
one person and nobody else is evidence about that person, and she treats it
that way.

What she brings to a casualty is the consequence, stated plainly and
without deciding the engineering: how long the crew in a space can keep
working, who has to come out now, and what she will need if the answer
arrives late.
What does Navarro conclude from symptoms in one compartment and not the others?
The evidence is about that compartment, not about the whole boat
The whole boat's atmosphere is degrading and that space showed it first
The people in that space are more susceptible than the rest of the crew
The monitors in the other compartments have failed
Engineering Watch Supervisor

Runs the plant: what turns the shaft, what cools what, and what every one
of those things gives away in noise. Eighteen years, most of them within
earshot of a reduction gear.

He thinks in dependency chains. A seawater pump cools a heat exchanger,
which cools a lubricating oil system, which is what lets a bearing carry a
shaft. Secure the pump to be quiet and you have started a clock on the
bearing, and the clock is not on any gauge in the room.

Noise is the other half of his job. Machinery that is loose, misaligned or
cavitating tells the whole ocean about it, and the sonar room hears the
boat's own faults before anybody in the engine room feels them. He and
Rask compare notes more than either department expects.
What has Haruki started when he secures a cooling pump to be quiet?
A clock on whatever that pump was cooling, which no gauge in the room shows
A drop in shaft speed that sonar will hear immediately
A loss of propulsion that must be reported before it happens
An automatic restart, once the temperature rises far enough
Propulsion Plant Operator

Stands the throttle watch, which is a job of small adjustments and long
attention. He knows the boat's speed curve by feel and can tell you what a
turn count costs in noise before the sonar room does.

His concern is cavitation: below a certain depth-and-speed combination the
propeller boils the water on its own blades, and the bubbles collapsing
are the loudest thing a submarine can do. Deeper water suppresses it,
because there is more pressure holding the bubbles shut. Faster brings it
on. The two trade off against each other, and the trade is the decision.

He is also the one who has to say no. An ordered speed that would make the
boat audible is a report to the officer of the deck, not a throttle
movement, and saying so is the job.
Why does going deeper let Adeyemi turn more shaft revolutions quietly?
More pressure holds the bubbles shut, so the propeller cavitates less
Colder water at depth muffles the propeller
The hull is stiffer at depth and transmits less noise
Sound travels more slowly deeper, so it carries less far
Commanding Officer

Has the boat. Every decision in this game eventually arrives on her table
as a choice between things that are all partly true, and she is the only
person aboard who cannot pass it on.

She works in a currency the departments do not: an hour spent confirming a
contact is an hour the boat has not moved, and an hour of transit is an
hour of exposure. What she asks for is never certainty. It is what is
known, what is not, and which of the two is about to change.

She is unimpressed by confidence and interested in evidence. A watch
officer who says "probably nothing" gets asked what would have to be true
for that to be wrong, and how expensive it would be to check.
What does Vance actually ask her watchstanders for?
The settled facts, the open ones, and which of them moves next
A single recommendation, with the reasoning left out
The most cautious option available, every time
Certainty before the boat commits to anything
Executive Officer

Runs the watch bill, the drills and the boat's time, which makes him the
person who decides what the crew is doing while a casualty is being
fought — and therefore what is not being watched.

His subject is delegation. There are more jobs than people in any real
casualty, and the mistake is not choosing wrong, it is choosing everything:
a boat where the whole crew is fighting a fire has nobody on sonar and
nobody on the plot, and it will hit something while it is winning.

He keeps the casualty log, which is the record of what was known when. It
is dull until the debrief, when it is the only thing that can tell the
difference between a bad decision and a decision that was right with the
information on the table.
What is Whitfield's objection to putting the whole crew on the casualty?
Nobody is left on sonar or the plot, and the boat can hit something while winning
A large team gets in each other's way in a small compartment
The relief watch will be too tired to take over
Damage control equipment is only issued to one team at a time
The direction to something, measured as an angle. Passive sonar gives you this and little else.
How fast a contact's bearing is changing. Near zero on a closing contact is the dangerous case.
The lowest part of a compartment, where water collects. Its level over time is the flooding rate.
Listening across all frequencies at once. Shows a contact as a smear that persists in bearing.
The gas the crew breathes out. It has to be removed continuously, because in a sealed boat it only accumulates.
Bubbles forming and collapsing on a propeller blade. The loudest ordinary thing a submarine does.
A valve in a ventilation duct. Its position decides which compartments share air with the plant.
Advancing a position from course, speed and time. It knows what the boat did and nothing about the water.
What stops working when you secure or isolate something else. The reason isolation is never free.
The kind of electrical supply a submarine runs on from its batteries: one steady direction, unlike the alternating supply ashore.
A position from a measurement rather than a calculation. Everything after it is dead reckoning again.
Listening at one frequency. Machinery makes lines here, and a line can identify what is making it.
A fire re-igniting after it looked out, because the ignition source was never removed.
The plant that removes carbon dioxide from the boat's air. It reaches only where the dampers let it.
The direction and speed the water is carrying the boat. Invisible to dead reckoning until measured.
The sound a boat makes that identifies it. Every machine running adds to it.
The boundary between warm surface water and cold water below. Sound bends at it, making shadow zones.
The element that turns sound in the water into a voltage, or a voltage into sound. An array is many of them listening together.
How the boat's weight is balanced fore and aft. Water taken aboard anywhere changes it.
Boat Walkdown
Learn the boat as a system of spaces, not a list of names.
You have the watch for the first time. Before anything else happens, you have to be able to find your way around this hull in the dark, and know what is in each space and how you would get out of it.

Two hours to sailing, alongside, and the fire main isolation valve in the forward compartment is chained shut with nobody willing to say who chained it. Chief Ferro wants to walk you through the boat before you take your first watch tonight. This watch you learn the forward spaces, what the fittings on a bulkhead are for, and how to get from one end of the boat to the other without looking at anything. Ferro's rule is that a route learned as a sequence survives being interrupted. Tonight you may have to find that valve in the dark, in smoke, by feel.
A compartment is defined by its boundaries, what it holds, and how you leave it.
What a walkdown is for
Learn a compartment in the order the facts depend on each other
Forward Equipment & Handling

Chief Ferro walks you into the forward space and asks you to learn it. Equipment down both sides, deck plates over a recess, a hose reel on the bulkhead, two ways out. He is not telling you what to take in first.
A compartment is a pressure boundary first; everything you learn about it hangs off that.
a submarine is divided into compartments that can be sealed off

A submarine survives a casualty by being divided, so the pressure boundary comes first: at ninety metres it is the difference between a flooded compartment and a flooded boat. The ways out come next, and they have to be proved rather than assumed. Then what in here could start a casualty — sea connections, cables, stores. And last, whether what is stored here can fight the casualty those things would start, because a locker is only the right locker once you know what this space can do to you.
The boundary first. It is what makes this a space rather than part of the next one, and everything after it is about what happens inside.
Both ways out second, and proved to open. A hatch that has not been tried is not a way out.
What could start a casualty third: sea connections, cables, stores. You cannot judge the equipment until you know the threat.
Whether this compartment can fight that casualty, last. It is a judgement about the first three, not a fifth fact.
Find where the pressure boundary runs, because it decides whether a casualty is this compartment's or the one aft.
Prove both hatches out of the compartment still open, by trying them.
Find what in here could start a casualty — sea connections, cables, stores.
Judge whether the equipment stowed here can fight a fire or a flood in this space.
Every fitting is an argument
Match each fitting to what it is there to do.
Propulsion Machinery
Chief Haruki stops beside four fittings on the same bulkhead and asks what each one is for. None is labelled with its purpose, only with its number.
What a fitting is for is decided by what is on the other side of it, and at what pressure.
pressure rises about one atmosphere for every ten metres of depth

What a fitting does comes from what it is connected to, and its shape is most of the clue when there is no time to trace a line. A wheel valve on a line through the pressure hull has the sea behind it, at ten atmospheres at ninety metres — which is why it is the one you never open to find out. A quick-connect manifold at head height is breathing air, so a space can be entered before its atmosphere is fit. A strapped locker holds shoring and plugs. A hose reel puts water on a fire.
Opening it at ninety metres admits the sea at ten atmospheres.
It supplies breathing air, so a space can be entered before its atmosphere is fit to breathe.
It holds the shoring and plugs that let this compartment fight its own casualty.
It puts water on a fire, and only once the circuit has been proved dead.
A wheel valve on a line through the pressure hull is the only one with the ocean on the far side. Depth sets what comes through it.
Quick-connect couplings at head height are breathing air — a supply for people, not for a system.
A strapped locker with a quick-release catch holds the shoring and plugs this compartment fights with.
A flat-folded hose on a reel is firefighting water, and it goes on only after the circuit has been proved dead.
A wheel valve on a line that passes through the pressure hull.
A manifold at head height with quick-connect couplings.
A strapped steel locker with a quick-release catch.
A flat-folded hose on a reel, beside a small isolating valve.
The trip back without a waypoint
Carry a message without a marker
Control Room

Nine compartments in a line, four of them with two doors, and one ladder aft. The navigator hands you a written message for machinery control, says the marker will be switched off for the walk back, and you have been through the boat once.
Dead reckoning fails at the interruption, so carry the thing that survives one.
submerged, there are no windows and no landmarks
What should you fix in your head before you set off?

Everything anybody aboard knows about where they are comes from keeping track since the last thing they were sure of. That is dead reckoning, and it is what the boat does with its own position between fixes. It fails at the interruption, and a boat is full of interruptions. A pace count does not survive stepping round somebody. A list of turns does not survive taking one extra. A stencilled number cannot be read with the lighting gone. An ordered list of spaces survives all three, because you can rejoin it anywhere.
The order of the compartments, since a sequence survives interruption.
The number of paces between hatches, because a count is exact.
The route as a list of turns, because turns are easy to hold.
The stencilled compartment numbers, because they are already written down.
Paces stop being useful the moment you have to step around somebody.
Deck colours vanish with the lighting, which is exactly when you need this.
Wandering works until the boat is dark or on fire, which is when it is asked for.
Contact in the Noise
Work out what is out there before the boat commits to anything.

Sonar has four sources on the display at once. Two of them have been there since before the boat slowed, one came with the turn, and one comes and goes. The captain wants to know which of them she has to care about.

Second day out, forenoon watch. Four traces on the broadband display, and the sonar supervisor, Nils Rask, has been arguing with his own operator about the fourth for eleven minutes: it holds almost the same bearing and it is getting louder. The captain, Commander Iris Vance, wants a classification before the boat commits to the track she has been ordered onto. This watch you sort out what is out there and say what a steady bearing means. Sound is all you have. And a bearing that does not change is not a quiet situation — it is the signature of two ships on converging courses.
A bearing is a measurement; a track is an argument built from several of them.
Four traces, one of them ours
Match each trace to what is making it.
Sonar Room
Four traces on the broadband display. The watch has been on for six minutes, the boat slowed four minutes ago, and one trace changed when it did.
A source that changes when the boat changes belongs to the boat.
passive sonar listens and does not transmit

Broadband hears everything radiating into the water: the ocean, the animals in it, the ships on it, and always the boat you are standing in. Sorting them is the first job, because nothing can be tracked until it is identified. A hiss that rises and falls with our own turn count belongs to us. A narrow line at a fixed frequency drifting slowly in bearing is a merchant's blade rate. Short chirps with no bearing rate are biologic. Two lines an octave apart on a bearing that barely moves, growing louder, is the dangerous one.
Own-ship machinery, because it follows our own throttle.
A merchant on a steady course, her blade rate showing as a line.
Biologic — it does not behave the way a hull has to.
A contact closing on a steady bearing, which is the dangerous one.
A source that follows our own throttle is ours. Nothing out in the water knows what our turn count is doing.
A narrow line at a fixed frequency, drifting slowly in bearing, is machinery on a ship holding a course.
Short chirps with no bearing rate, gone in a minute, do not behave the way a hull has to. That is life, not a contact.
Two lines an octave apart on a steady bearing, getting louder, is something closing. Steady bearing plus rising level is the one to say out loud.
A steady hiss whose level rises and falls with our own turn count.
A narrow line at a fixed frequency, drifting slowly in bearing.
Short chirps with no bearing rate at all, gone within a minute.
Two lines an octave apart, bearing barely moving, growing louder.
The trace that will not resolve
Which explanation fits every reading, not just the loudest one?
Sonar Room
The fourth trace is faint, has held nearly the same bearing for eleven minutes, and does not appear on narrowband at all. The boat has not changed speed or depth since it appeared.
Evidence that survives a change in your own state is evidence about the world.
sound bends when it crosses water of a different temperature
A faint trace has held the same bearing for eleven minutes and shows nothing on narrowband.

Broadband hears the total sound a thing makes; narrowband picks out the pure tones machinery produces at fixed frequencies, which is usually how a contact gets a name. So a missing line is evidence, not a blank space where evidence should be. Sound in the ocean does not travel straight — a temperature layer bends it, and a path bent through the layer arrives faint and stripped of its detail. Eleven minutes of persistence rules out noise and biologics, and nothing of ours changed, so it is not ours.
A quiet contact past the layer
Sound from above the layer bends away, arriving faint and without its machinery lines.
Own-ship noise
Something aboard is making it, and it would have changed when we did.
Biologic
A living source, which would come and go rather than hold a bearing for eleven minutes.
A display artefact
The processor drawing a line where there is no sound at all.
Nothing to explain
Ordinary noise that happens to look like a line.
Something of ours would have changed when we did, and nothing aboard has changed in eleven minutes.
A biologic comes and goes. This has held nearly the same bearing for eleven minutes.
A display artefact is a line drawn where there is no sound. Broadband is hearing something; narrowband simply is not.
There is something to explain: a faint trace that persists on a steady bearing is the shape of a contact, not of noise.
The bearing that does not move
Say what a steady bearing means
Control Room
The contact's bearing has changed by less than half a degree in six minutes, and it is getting louder. The officer of the deck asks what that means for the boat.
A constant bearing with a rising level is a collision geometry, not a quiet one.
passive sonar gives a direction and no range at all
What does a steady bearing and a rising level tell you?

A bearing and how it behaves over time is the only ranging instrument a quiet boat has, which makes relative motion the whole trade. Two ships whose relative bearing does not change are closing along a straight line between them — it is the oldest rule at sea and it needs no range. A stopped contact's bearing would swing as we moved past it. An opening contact gets quieter, not louder. Waiting for a range spends the six minutes the geometry has already given you.
We are on a collision course, and the range is closing.
The contact is stopped, since its bearing is not changing.
The contact is opening, and the level is rising for another reason.
Nothing until a range is available.
A stopped contact's bearing would change as we moved past it.
An opening contact gets quieter, not louder.
Waiting for a range wastes the six minutes the geometry just gave you.
Position Without a Trusted Fix
Work out not where the boat is, but how well that is known.

The boat has been submerged for hours on dead reckoning. The plot is a confident-looking line drawn from course and speed, and it knows nothing about the water that has been setting the boat sideways the whole time. Ahead is a bank.

Third day, middle watch, and the last trusted fix was three and a half hours ago. The navigator, Imani Sowande, has the plot built from course, speed and time, her assistant Anya Petrov has been reading the depth sounder, and the two of them do not agree. There is a current here of about half a knot that nobody has measured today. This watch you work out how far the water has carried the boat, decide which instrument to believe, and get a position that does not depend on the plot at all. Two displays taking their heading from the same gyro will agree beautifully, which is Sowande's whole worry. Sixty fathoms, and a bank half a mile off the track.
Precision is not accuracy, and two displays sharing a source are one measurement.
How far the water has carried us
Age the position
Control Room
The last trusted fix was three and a half hours ago. The forecast set for this area is about half a knot, and nobody has applied it to the plot because nobody has measured it.
Dead reckoning tells you where you would be if nothing pushed you.
the log measures speed through the water, not over the ground
Estimate how far the boat could be from where the plot says it is.

Between fixes the boat's position is dead reckoning: course, speed and time worked forward from the last certainty. But the water moves as well, and a current carries the whole boat sideways without registering on a single instrument aboard. Half a knot for three and a half hours is not a rounding error — it is nearly two miles of set that the plot cannot see, and the error grows every hour it goes unmeasured. This is the plot the route through the narrows will be drawn on.
The set has been running about half a knot since the last trusted fix.
Estimate how far the boat could be from the plotted position.
Distance is rate times time, and the rate here is the water, not the boat. Own speed is what the plot already knows about; it is not part of the error.
Distance = speed × time. A knot is one nautical mile per hour.
Two displays, one source
Which explanation accounts for every reading here?
Control Room
The chart overlay and the electronic repeat agree to within a hundred yards. The depth sounder says the water is twelve metres shallower than the chart shows for that position. There is a bank ahead.
Independent confirmation only counts when the second source can fail differently.
two instruments can share a source and therefore share its errors
The two navigation displays agree exactly, and the bottom does not agree with either.

Agreement between instruments feels like confirmation, and it is only worth something when the two could have failed in different ways. These two are fed by one inertial navigator, so they agree by construction — they could not disagree if the navigator were wrong. The depth sounder is not part of that arrangement at all: it is looking straight down at something outside the boat. The temperature-depth trace shows 14 degrees down to 60 metres and 9 below it. The contact was held for forty minutes at 20 metres' depth on this boat, then gone in a single sweep, with every other trace on the display unchanged.

The route ahead narrows between the bank and a shipping lane. Command wants the boat through it with contact held throughout and as little acoustic exposure as the plant allows.

Take the own-noise baseline, because nothing new can be recognised as new without it.

The narrows are four miles across. The plot's uncertainty is a circle about two miles wide, and the bank is on the left-hand side of the channel.

a plotted position is the centre of a probability, not a fact
How much clear water is left if the boat runs the middle of the channel?

The circle drawn round a plotted position is the honest width of where the boat might actually be, so planning a route is arithmetic done on the circle rather than on the pencil line. Four miles of channel, and a position that could be a mile out either way.

Margin = half the channel width − half the position uncertainty.

Machinery Room
At 92 revolutions the after compartment rings loudly enough to hear through a bulkhead. At 85 and at 100 it does not. Nothing else about the plant changes between them.
A compartment has standing-wave frequencies of its own, and forcing it at one of them is what makes it loud.
every structure has frequencies at which it prefers to vibrate
The hull rings at one shaft speed and nowhere else. Why that one?

A compartment supports standing waves, and a forcing frequency that coincides with one of them is amplified, sometimes by an order of magnitude, and away from it the same forcing is unremarkable. Blade rate is shaft speed times the number of blades, so one particular revolution count lands on the compartment's resonance and its neighbours do not. That is why the fix is a shaft speed to avoid, or a mount that shifts the resonance, rather than more power or a quieter crew.
At that speed the blade rate matches a natural frequency of the structure, so the response is amplified.

The bearing is failing, and a failing bearing is loudest in the middle of its range.
Cavitation begins at that speed and stops above it.

The forward space is taking water. The drain pump is running and the level is still rising. Somewhere under those deck plates is a hole, and the boat is at ninety metres, which is what makes it a hole worth respecting.

Sixth day, morning watch, and water is over the bilge in the forward space with the drain pump running. Ruth Hallam, on the pumps, has the level and reports it steady. Flooding is stopped at the hull fitting; everything else is delay.
Under the deck plates

Water is over the bilge in the forward space and the level is still rising with the drain pump running. The space carries a seawater supply header, a fresh water line and the sonar cooling return: three systems, one puddle.

sea pressure at depth is far higher than anything inside the boat

Water aboard is not only weight. It is a leak whose behaviour depends on where it came from, and a sea connection at ninety metres is fed by the entire ocean at about ten atmospheres. What the water is, and what has not changed on the systems around it, is the evidence that names the source. Salt rules out the fresh water line, whose tank level is unchanged anyway. The pump running backwards, which would show as a falling discharge pressure.

Forward Equipment & Handling

Flooding is a race between two rates, and both can be measured rather than argued about. The level rise gives what is accumulating; adding back what the pump is removing gives what the sea is actually putting in. That is why 'the drain pump is running' answers nothing on its own — pump output is not a fixed number, it falls as the head rises. The level went from 31 cm to 39 cm in one minute in a space this wide, with the drain pump already running.
Estimate the rate the sea is actually coming in at.

The rise is what is left after the pump has done its work, so the leak is the rise plus the pump — well over a hundred gallons a minute. The pump is not going to win, and knowing that is what sends somebody to the hull valve instead of for another pump.

Same day, afternoon watch, eight hours after the flooding and nobody has slept. Smoke from a switchboard in the electrical space. Three legs, three different actions
Match each leg of the fire to the action that removes it.
Electrical Distribution
Chief Okonkwo puts the three legs of the fire on the board. The fault that keeps lighting it, the insulation that burns, the air in the compartment. He asks what removes each one.
Each leg of a fire is a different action, and they are not interchangeable.
a fire needs fuel, oxygen and a source of energy

An electrical fire is the awkward case, because the energy keeps arriving down a cable from somewhere else in the boat. Removing the ignition source is what makes everything else hold — open the breaker, then prove the cable dead with a meter, because the switchboard reports a belief and the meter reports the conductor. The burning insulation is cooled below its re-light temperature. The air is cut off by shutting ventilation, and submerged that air is also what the crew breathes for the rest of the patrol. Open the breaker, then prove the cable dead with a meter.
Cool it below the temperature at which it re-lights.
Shut the ventilation to the space so the fire stops being fed.
Set and read boundaries with an infrared thermometer.
The energised fault is removed by opening the breaker and then proving the cable dead. Until it is dead, everything else is fighting a symptom.

The cable insulation that is actually burning.
The air in the compartment feeding the flame.
The heat conducting through the bulkhead to the next space.

An indicator lamp reports what the switchboard believes: a contact somewhere, a lamp that can fail, a bus that can be back-fed. Water on an energised cable puts the fault straight into the people holding the hose, so metering between opening and entering is the whole lesson — here the lamp and the cable disagreed, and a team that trusts the lamp goes in with the fault still live. Open the breaker for the affected bus.
Meter the cable in the compartment and confirm it is dead.
Enter with breathing protection and fight the fire.
Set boundaries and read them until the seat is cold.
Restore loads in dependency order, vital equipment first.

Breathing apparatus solves exactly one problem — the air — and leaves every other one untouched. Smoke takes away the instrument the team was actually using to find the fire, which is their own eyes. In a space that cannot be read by sight, the boundaries have to be measured instead: an infrared reading on the bulkhead is the only thing that says where the heat is. Nothing, as long as everybody is on breathing protection.

A fire consuming the air also produces carbon monoxide, which is worse, not self-solving.
Abandoning it hands the compartment to the fire, and the boundaries still need reading.

Navarro wants to know how long the space can be left before she pulls people out of it. Berthing holds nine people off watch and the compartment's volume is on the board.

A sealed volume divided by a production rate is a deadline in hours instead of an argument about whether it feels stuffy. Nine people, each producing about 0.04 cubic metres of CO₂ an hour, in a sealed space.

The volume and the target concentration give how much gas it takes; the people and their rate give how fast it arrives. An hour is not an emergency and it is not comfortable either, which is exactly the kind of answer that changes what you do next.

One fan feeds both the scrubber and the after spaces. What does that mean for the plan?

The ventilation drawing shows one fan feeding the scrubber and the after spaces through a common trunk. The watch bill treats them as two independent systems, and the atmosphere plan assumes both.

One fan feeds both the scrubber and the after spaces. What does that mean for the plan?

Redundancy is not about how many systems are drawn on the diagram, it is about what they share. Two paths through one fan fail together, and a plan that assumes they are independent has no answer for the case that actually happens. The work is to find the shared component, decide whether a second path exists, and if it does not, write down what the boat will do instead — before the failure, while the decision is still cheap.
The fan is a single point of failure, and the plan needs a second path or a stated fallback.
Nothing. Two systems on one fan is normal and the fan is reliable.

The after spaces should be sealed off, since they are downstream.

Sealing the after spaces removes them from the plan rather than protecting them, and people are berthed there.

Command is deciding what you do, and who does the rest.
Four casualties, one crew
Decide what is first

Water forward, a bus lost aft, the plot degraded by the power loss, and a crewman with a broken wrist in the passage. Every one of them has somebody standing in front of you asking about it.

The flooding, because it is the only one that gets worse by itself.

The watch bill exists so one person's attention is never what limits the boat. What Whitfield needs is not a description of each problem but a first action, and the pairings are not obvious from the department. The lost bus is answered by proving what is actually dead with a meter, because the switchboard only reports what it believes. The plot is fixed by slowing the boat before anybody plots anything. The injured man is moved because the passage is a damage-control route. The bulkheads are read on both sides, which is how you learn the boundary is holding.

The crewman with a broken wrist, in the passage.
The plot, degraded since the power went.
The bulkheads either side of the flooded space.

The boat is making eight knots toward a bank nine miles away, with a plot that has been degraded for six minutes.

Time is the only resource in a casualty that can be manufactured, and speed is the price list. Nine miles at eight knots is a little over an hour; the same nine miles at three knots is three. An hour is not enough time to fight a flooding casualty and rebuild a plot. Three hours is. The boat's speed is the one number on this list that you control, and it is worth two hours.

Which explanation fits the whole picture?

Broadband is up across the whole display rather than in one sector. A new narrowband line has appeared at a frequency that is not a round number, and it moved slightly when the plant changed.

Two narrowband lines, 147 and 150 hertz, and the operator says the level swells and dies three times a second on the audio. The display shows two steady lines and nothing else.
Two tones close together rise and fall together at a rate you can hear and count.
two waves arriving together add where they are in phase and cancel where they are not
Two lines three hertz apart, and the amplitude rises and falls three times a second. What is it?

Two tones close in frequency drift in and out of phase with each other, adding where they agree and cancelling where they do not, and they come back into phase at the difference frequency — 150 minus 147, three times a second. So the pulsing is not a third signal and not an artefact: it is evidence that there are exactly two sources, and their spacing is measurable by ear. Sonar Room — three displays and a dark space, because the eye recovers faster than the ear does. Everything the boat knows about the world outside the hull arrives here first.
Control Room — the plot, the planes and the periscope. The boat is driven from here, and the chart table is where a position stops being a calculation and becomes a decision.
Propulsion Machinery — what turns the shaft, and the loudest compartment aboard. Everything in this space is a trade between speed and being heard.
Electrical Distribution — the switchboard and every cable run in the boat. A fire in here is a fire with a power supply, which is a different problem from a fire.
Forward Equipment & Handling — the working space at the bow, and the reason flooding is a forward problem: the sea connections for the forward systems are here, under the deck plates.
Sonar-Array Electronics — the cabinets that turn what the array hears into something a person can read. They need cooling water, which is why a flooding casualty forward is also a sonar casualty.
Radio & Communications — where the boat would talk to anybody, which submerged it mostly does not. Coming up to transmit is a decision about exposure, not about equipment.
Berthing, Mess & Medical — where the crew that is not on watch is, which makes it the compartment where atmosphere problems show up as people before they show up as numbers.
Machinery Control Room — the plant is run from here rather than from beside it. Every gauge in this space is a report from somewhere else in the boat.
